6T SRAM cell: what goes wrong, specs, and design guide

2026-11-05

Why it is not just two inverters

The 6T cell is hard because the same two access transistors must be weak enough that a read cannot flip the cell, yet strong enough that a write must flip it. Every other difficulty (Vmin, yield, assists) comes from squeezing those opposite demands into the smallest transistors on the die, repeated a billion times, with 6-sigma variation.

Devices: pull-downs PD1/PD2 (NMOS), pull-ups PU1/PU2 (PMOS), pass-gates PG1/PG2 (NMOS, gate = wordline WL, drain = BL / BLB). Nodes Q and QB.

Inverter 1 is PU1 + PD1: its output is Q and its input (the tied gates) is QB. Inverter 2 is PU2 + PD2: output QB, input Q. PG1 joins Q to BL and PG2 joins QB to BLB; both gates sit on WL.

Convention for the rest of the doc: in read examples the cell stores Q = 0, QB = 1, so the read current flows from BL through PG1 and PD1, and "the other inverter" means PU2/PD2. In write examples Q starts at 1 and BL is driven to 0, so PG1 fights PU1.

ModeWLBitlinesWhat must happenWhich ratio decides it
Hold0Precharged or floatingLatch keeps state, leaks littleInverter gain, leakage
Read1Both precharged to VDD, floatingThe '0' node (say Q) discharges BL through PG1 and PD1 but Q must rise only a little (the read bump)Cell ratio beta = (W/L)PD / (W/L)PG, typically 1.5 to 2.5
Write1One driven to 0 (BL), other at VDDTo write 0 into Q (Q=1 now), BL=0 and PG1 pulls Q down against PU1 until Q falls below the trip point of the PU2/PD2 inverterPull-up ratio gamma = (W/L)PU / (W/L)PG, typically 0.5 to 1

So the sizing chain is PD strongest, PG middle, PU weakest. Read wants PG weak; write wants PG strong. That one transistor is the whole design tension, and it is why modern SRAM leans on assist circuits instead of sizing alone.

What can go wrong

There are six classic failures. The first four are functional (a wrong bit), the last two are parametric (too slow or too leaky), and all of them are dominated by local Vt mismatch rather than by the nominal design.

  1. Read disturb (read upset). With WL high, the '0' node Q sits at the midpoint of a divider: PG1 from the precharged BL pushing up, PD1 pulling down. Q rises to a read bump of roughly VDD x 1/(1+beta) in a crude linear model, usually 100 to 200 mV. If that bump crosses the trip point of the PU2/PD2 inverter, QB falls and the cell flips. Worst case: weak PD1, strong PG1, low trip point of the other inverter (strong PD2 or weak PU2 relative), high VDD on BL, FS or SF corners, hot or cold depending on process.

    • Measured by read SNM (RSNM): the butterfly curve with WL=1, BL=BLB=VDD. Typically only 20 to 40 percent of hold SNM.

  2. Write failure. PG cannot overpower PU, so the '1' node never drops below the trip point within the WL pulse. Worst case: strong PU, weak PG, low VDD, SF corner (slow N, fast P), and low temperature in many processes. It can also be a timing failure: the node gets there but too late for the pulse width.

    • Measured by write margin (WM): e.g. the BL voltage at which the cell flips with the other BL at VDD, or the WL voltage needed to flip it.

  3. Hold or retention failure. In standby, especially at reduced data-retention voltage (DRV), the two inverters lose gain, mismatch tilts the butterfly until one lobe closes, and the cell falls into a single stable state. Also caused by supply noise or by excessive leakage from the '1' node through PD and PG.

    • Measured by hold SNM and by DRV (the lowest VDD that still holds data at the target sigma).

  4. Half-select disturb. In a column-muxed array, WL turns on a whole row, but only some columns are being written. The unselected cells on that row see a pseudo-read: precharged bitlines and an open PG. So every write also performs a read-stability test on its neighbours. Column-select on the BL or interleaving is what creates this; it is also why write-assist schemes that raise WL hurt read stability of half-selected cells.

  5. Access time or read current failure (too slow). Read current Iread through PG+PD discharges a heavily loaded BL (hundreds of cells, each adding junction capacitance plus wire). The sense amp needs a differential, say 50 to 150 mV, by the time it fires. A weak cell (low Iread tail) or a high leakage BL (all other cells on the column leaking through their PGs onto the opposite BL) means the differential is too small or of the wrong sign. This sets the bitline-to-cells ratio and the sense-amp offset budget.

  6. Leakage. Each cell has subthreshold leakage through the off PU, off PD and off PG, plus gate and GIDL leakage. Multiply by 10^8 cells and it dominates standby power. Low-leakage (high-Vt) cells help leakage and read stability but hurt Iread and write.

Cross-cutting causes, illustrated

These five effects never show up in a nominal TT simulation, but they decide whether the cell works. Every figure below comes from a generic teaching model: an EKV-style MOS with velocity saturation, Vt = 0.35 V, beta = 1.5, PU = PG, and VDD = 1.0 V unless noted. The model is in sram_model.py and the figures are drawn by make_figs.py. The trends carry over to real silicon. The numbers are not your PDK's.

1. Local Vt mismatch: the butterfly loses its symmetry

Mechanism. Every transistor gets its own random Vt from random dopants, line-edge roughness and metal-gate grain. Pelgrom's law gives sigma(Vt) = AVt / sqrt(W x L), and SRAM uses near-minimum devices, so this spread is as large as it gets. A global corner moves all six devices together, so both halves shift identically and the butterfly stays mirror-symmetric. Local mismatch moves each half on its own.

How the curve moves. The figure makes one cell "bad" by weakening PD1 (+50 mV) and strengthening PG1 (-50 mV). Only half 1 changes, so only curve B (orange, Q = f1(QB)) moves.

  • A weaker PD1 raises inverter 1's trip point, so the flat part of curve B lifts, from about 0.45 to 0.48 V.

  • In read, the stronger PG1 and weaker PD1 also raise the read bump, so the left wall of the upper-left lobe moves right.

  • The upper-left lobe, which protects a stored 0, is squeezed from both sides and falls from 287 to 247 mV. The lower-right lobe, which protects a stored 1, gains room and grows to 307 mV.

  • Rule: a Vt shift in one half slides that half's curve, and one lobe loses roughly what the other gains. SNM is the smaller lobe, so mismatch always hurts.

  • In hold, PG is off, so only the trip-point shift acts: 432 against 461 mV.

Which device matters. Each bar is the change in read SNM per +1 mV of Vt on one device, where a higher Vt means a weaker device. For the lobe of a stored 0 (blue):

  • A weak PD1 hurts most, at -0.41 mV/mV, because the bump rises.

  • A weak PG1 helps, at +0.35, because the bump falls.

  • A weak PD2 helps, at +0.41, because it raises Vm2, the threshold the bump has to reach.

  • A weak PU2 hurts, at -0.18, because it lowers Vm2.

  • PU1 and PG2 barely matter for that lobe.

The stored-1 lobe (orange) is the exact mirror. Interview line: read stability is set by PD against PG on the 0 side, and by the trip point of the opposite inverter.

Monte Carlo. 3000 cells, each with six random Vt values (sigma = 30 mV for a 1-unit device, divided by sqrt(W)). RSNM comes out at a mean of 273 mV with sigma 13 mV. The 6-sigma cell is a 1-in-a-billion event, so none of the 3000 samples is anywhere near it. You fit the distribution and quote mean - 6 sigma, here 195 mV. Real tails are often worse than Gaussian, so production sign-off uses importance sampling or scaled-sigma sampling rather than trusting the fit.

2. Why everything is quoted in sigma

A per-cell failure probability p, over N bits, gives an array yield of exactly (1 - p)^N, the chance that every bit is good. Since p is tiny, ln(1 - p) is about -p, so this equals exp(-N x p): the Poisson chance of zero failures when N x p failures are expected. For 99 percent of arrays to work with no repair, p has to be about 0.01/N. That is 5.6 sigma for 1 Mb, 6.3 sigma for 64 Mb and 6.7 sigma for 1 Gb. Every extra decade of bits costs only about a quarter of a sigma, but each sigma is worth tens of mV of margin, which is why SRAM teams fight for single millivolts. Spare rows and columns plus ECC let a few cells fail, which relaxes the requirement by very roughly half to one sigma.

3. Aging: the cell weakens against the data it holds

Mechanism. BTI (bias temperature instability): a transistor that sits on with its gate under stress builds up interface and oxide traps, so its |Vt| rises. That is NBTI on PMOS and PBTI on high-k NMOS. A cell storing Q = 0 for years keeps PU2 on (gate = Q = 0, NBTI) and PD1 on (gate = QB = 1, PBTI), while PU1 and PD2 sit off and unstressed. So aging behaves like a mismatch that grows with time and always points against the stored state. The figure uses +50 mV on PU2 and +25 mV on PD1 at 10 years, growing as t^0.2.

What gets worse, and how. Both stressed devices are the bad ones from the sensitivity chart above: a weak PD1 raises the bump and a weak PU2 lowers Vm2.

  • After 10 years, the read lobe of the stored 0 shrinks from 287 to 268 mV. The opposite lobe grows to 298 mV.

  • The write margin to overwrite that 0 rises from 254 to 278 mV, because a weaker PU2 makes QB easier to pull down. So an old cell is less stable when read and easier to flip.

  • With a t^0.2 law, half of the 10-year shift happens in the first 10 yr x 0.5^5, about 4 months. Burn-in and the first months of use do most of the damage.

  • BTI partly recovers once the stress is removed. That is one reason some designs periodically invert the stored data.

  • Hot-carrier injection on PG, from millions of read and write pulses, weakens PG and lowers the read current over life. This model's PG is not aged, so its Iread barely moves (about 1 percent). In silicon, expect access time to slow down.

  • Sign-off: Vmin is checked with end-of-life (aged) models, not only fresh ones.

4. Soft errors: charge from a particle strike

Mechanism. An alpha particle or a neutron leaves a track of electron-hole pairs. The reverse-biased drain of an off NMOS sitting on the '1' node (PD1 when Q = 1) collects that charge as a current pulse, which pulls Q down. Two things race: PU1 trying to restore Q, and the feedback through inverter 2 trying to latch the new value.

  • At 0.95 x Qcrit, Q dips to about 0.36 V, stays above inverter 2's trip point, and recovers.

  • At 1.05 x Qcrit, Q crosses the trip point, QB rises, and the cell latches the wrong value within about 75 ps.

  • Qcrit is about 1.7 fC with 1 fF nodes at 1.0 V and scales roughly with VDD, down to 0.56 fC at 0.5 V. Low-voltage and smaller cells are easier to upset.

  • Fixes: ECC plus bit interleaving (so one strike hits several words, one bit in each), more node capacitance, or hardened cells such as DICE.

5. Power-up state

At power-up the cell falls into whichever state its mismatch favours. That doesn't matter for a memory, and it is the basis of SRAM PUFs in security. Tests and firmware must never assume a default value.

Specs you design to

The spec that matters is not a nominal margin but the margin at the yield target: mean minus k sigma, with k around 6, at the worst corner and temperature. A cell that looks fine at TT 27C nominal tells you almost nothing.

MetricDefinitionHow to simulateTypical target (order of magnitude)
Hold SNM (HSNM)Side of the largest square that fits in the smaller lobe of the butterfly, WL=0DC sweep each inverter's VTC, overlay one mirrored30 to 40 percent of VDD nominal; mean-6sigma > 0 at DRV
Read SNM (RSNM)Same, with WL=VDD and BL=BLB=VDD loading each inverterDC sweep with PG on; or N-curvemean/sigma > 6; often 100 to 200 mV nominal at 0.8 to 1 V
N-curve SINM / SVNMCurrent and voltage noise margins from injecting current at Q while sweeping V(Q)DC current sweep, read modePositive at 6 sigma; better than SNM because it includes current capability
Write margin (WM)BL voltage (or WL voltage) at which the cell flipsDC sweep BL from VDD down with WL on; or WL sweepWrite trip point well above 0 V, mean-6sigma > 0
Write timeWL rise to node crossingTransientFits the WL pulse with margin
IreadCurrent through PG+PD with Q=0, WL=VDD, BL=VDDDCLow tail (mean-6sigma) gives enough dV on BL by sense time
Ileak (cell)Total standby current per cellDC, WL=0, hot corner (FF 125C)pA per cell; total array budget in uA to mA
VminLowest VDD at which read, write and hold all pass at the yield targetSweep VDD, take the max of the three failure VDDsSets the low-voltage operating point of the whole chip
DRVLowest standby VDD that retains dataHold SNM vs VDDWell below Vmin; used for retention mode
Qcrit / SERCharge to flip a node; FIT rateTransient current pulse at QPaired with ECC spec
Cell areaum^2 per bitLayoutFoundry thin-cell, set by pushed rules

Ratio guidelines (starting points, always confirm with sigma analysis):

  • beta = (W/L)PD / (W/L)PG from about 1.2 to 2.5 for read stability. Higher is more stable but bigger and harder to write.

  • gamma = (W/L)PU / (W/L)PG from about 0.5 to 1 for writability. In FinFET these become integer fin ratios such as PU:PG:PD = 1:1:1 (high density, beta = 1, so stability comes from Vt choice and assists) or 1:2:2 (high current).

  • Vmin is usually set by read stability at the slow-fast corners and by write at low temperature, so you report Vmin as the max of Vmin_read, Vmin_write, Vmin_hold.

How Vmin falls out of the margins.

The figure sweeps VDD from 0.45 to 1.15 V. At each point it runs Monte Carlo: 200 cells for HSNM and RSNM, 80 for write margin, where WM is the BL voltage at which the cell flips. Each metric is drawn as its mean (solid) and its mean - 6 sigma (dashed).

  • Every margin shrinks as VDD drops, but the spread from mismatch does not shrink with it. Each metric's Vmin is where its dashed line hits zero.

  • In this cell, write is the limit: the 6-sigma cell can no longer be written with BL = 0 V below about 0.80 V. Read reaches zero only around 0.45 V, and hold never limits in this range.

  • The write spread is large because WM depends on PU fighting PG, two small devices with independent mismatch. (The write curve is estimated from only 80 samples, so treat it as rough.)

  • Chip Vmin is the highest of the read, write and hold Vmins, plus guard bands for aging and noise. Raising beta moves the read Vmin down and the write Vmin up. That trade-off is why assists exist (see the design guide).

What SNM is and how to read it off a butterfly

Static noise margin (SNM) is the largest DC noise voltage the cell can take on its two internal nodes before it loses its state. On the butterfly plot, it is the side of the largest square that fits inside the smaller lobe. In the sample below (a generic model, not your PDK, beta = 1.5, VDD = 1.0 V), that square is 441 mV in hold and 287 mV in read.

The two curves. Curve A is QB = f2(Q), inverter 2 with its input on the x-axis (Cadence "btb vs bt"). Curve B is Q = f1(QB), inverter 1 drawn with its axes swapped so that its input QB sits on the y-axis ("bt vs btb"). Each curve is an ordinary single-valued VTC. The cell can only rest where both are true at once, which is where the curves cross. That gives three points: two stable corners, one per lobe, and the metastable point on the diagonal.

Why the margin is a square. Put a DC noise source Vn in series with each inverter's input, with the polarity that hurts most. Curve A slides right by Vn and curve B slides up by Vn, so the two curves close in on each other along the diagonal. A lobe survives as long as a square of side Vn still fits inside it. Once Vn exceeds that side, the lobe closes, the curves cross only once, and the cell can hold only one value. Whatever it stored on the closed side flips.

Why it is the smaller lobe. Each lobe protects one stored value. The upper-left lobe protects Q = 0 and the lower-right lobe protects Q = 1. A cell is only as good as its weaker state. In the global-corner plots both lobes are mirror images, but local mismatch makes them unequal, and the smaller one is the spec.

How to get the number.

  1. By eye: fit the biggest square into each lobe, with one corner on each curve, and take the smaller side. That is how the corner table below was read, to within about 20 mV.

  2. Exactly, by rotating 45 degrees: u = (x − y)/√2 and v = (x + y)/√2. In these coordinates both curves are single-valued in u. For each lobe, take the largest gap in v between the two curves, then divide it by √2. That gap is the square's diagonal, the dotted line in the figure. snm_explained.py does this, and the same function works on a CSV export from Cadence.

  3. Directly in simulation: insert the two DC sources Vn into the broken feedback loop and sweep Vn until the cell flips. This is the textbook Seevinck setup and needs no post-processing.

Hold vs read. In read, PG1 drags the '0' node up to the read bump, and PD has to fight PU and PG together, so the low tail of each VTC sags. Both lobes lose their corners and shrink, which is why RSNM is usually 40 to 70 percent of HSNM and why read, not hold, usually sets Vmin. The second figure also sweeps beta: a stronger PD lowers the bump and raises RSNM.

Reading your butterfly curves

These are hold butterflies (WL off), and they say the cell holds data comfortably at every corner and temperature you ran. The worst hold margin comes from the skewed corners (FNSP, SNFP), not from SS or FF, and it drops to about a third of VDD at 0.7 V. They cannot yet tell you anything about read stability, write, or mismatch, which are the cases that actually set Vmin.

Node names: bt = Q and btb = QB in the schematic above. "btb vs bt" is inverter 2's VTC (QB as a function of Q). "bt vs btb" is inverter 1's VTC drawn with its axes swapped, which is what makes the two lobes.

1. How to tell these are hold curves. Each low level reaches 0 V and each high level reaches VDD. In a read butterfly (WL = VDD, BL = BLB = VDD) the low branch would not reach 0 V. It would sit on the read bump, roughly 0.1 to 0.2 V, and the lobes would shrink visibly. So these numbers are HSNM, and RSNM still has to be simulated.

2. The two lobes are always mirror images. A global corner moves all six devices the same way, so both inverters shift together and the plot stays symmetric about the line y = x. The cell has no preferred state here. A real failure needs local mismatch to make one lobe smaller than the other, so these runs are the baseline for Monte Carlo, not the sign-off.

3. What sets hold SNM: where the trip point sits, and how sharp the knees are. The upper-left lobe is roughly the box from 0 to Vm on x and from Vm to VDD on y, where Vm is the trip point where the curves cross on the diagonal. That limits the square to min(Vm, VDD − Vm). The rounded knees take a further bite off that. Eyeballed from TT at 1.0 V: Vm is about 0.48 V and HSNM is about 0.38 V, roughly 38 percent of VDD.

4. Your trip point sits below VDD/2, and that is the beta sizing showing up. At TT, Vm is about 0.35, 0.48 and 0.58 V at 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 V. The PD is sized strong for read stability and the PU weak for writability, so each inverter trips early. FNSP (fast NMOS, slow PMOS) pushes Vm down even further, and that is why it is the worst corner in your process-variation plot (Vm about 0.36 V at 1 V). SNFP pushes Vm the other way: at 1.3 V that actually centers it, but at 0.7 and 1.0 V it overshoots past VDD/2.

5. Temperature has a second-order effect in hold. Across -40 to 125 C, Vm moves by about 30 to 60 mV, and hot runs have softer knees. So the worst hold cases are FNSP hot (lowest Vm) and SNFP cold (highest Vm). TT, SS and FF barely change the margin.

6. Lower VDD costs more than the corner does. At 0.7 V the devices are close to threshold, the knees round off, and the transition widens compared with VDD. The margin falls faster than VDD scales once you add the skewed corners. This is the start of the DRV story.

Eyeballed trip point Vm and the ceiling on HSNM, min(Vm, VDD − Vm), near room temperature (plus or minus about 20 mV from reading the plots by eye; add the temperature spread from point 5):

Corner0.7 V: Vm / ceiling1.0 V: Vm / ceiling1.3 V: Vm / ceiling
TT0.35 / 0.35 (50%)0.48 / 0.48 (48%)0.58 / 0.58 (45%)
SS0.37 / 0.33 (47%)0.50 / 0.50 (50%)0.61 / 0.61 (47%)
FF0.34 / 0.34 (49%)0.46 / 0.46 (46%)0.55 / 0.55 (42%)
FNSP0.24 / 0.24 (34%)0.36 / 0.36 (36%)0.47 / 0.47 (36%)
SNFP0.46 / 0.24 (34%)0.61 / 0.39 (39%)0.70 / 0.60 (46%)

What to run next to turn this into a sign-off view:

  • Export the waveforms as CSV so HSNM can be extracted exactly (rotate the plot 45 degrees and take the largest square in each lobe) instead of read by eye.

  • Read butterfly: the same sweep with WL = VDD and BL = BLB = VDD. Expect the lobes to shrink sharply, with FS/SF and hot as the worst cases.

  • Write margin: WL = VDD, BL swept from VDD to 0, BLB = VDD.

  • Local mismatch Monte Carlo at the worst corner (FNSP hot, 0.7 V): fit the mean and sigma of the smaller lobe.

  • Check that the transient ramp is slow enough to count as DC, or switch to a .dc sweep (the plots say tran over 10 to 13 us).

The plots

Crossing values are read off the plots by eye at mid temperature (plus or minus about 20 mV). The ceiling is min(Vm, VDD − Vm).

PlotWhat to look at
1.0 V, all five corners, room temperature. TT, SS and FF cross at about 0.46 to 0.50 V, so their lobes are nearly the same size. FNSP crosses lowest, at about 0.36 V, which gives the smallest lobe and makes it the worst corner. SNFP crosses at about 0.61 V, for a ceiling of about 0.39 V. In every corner the two lobes stay mirror images of each other.
0.7 V TT. Crosses at about 0.35 V, right at VDD/2. The knees are rounder than at 1.0 V because the devices are close to threshold and have less gain, so the real HSNM falls further below the 0.35 V ceiling. Hot runs shift the crossing about 30 mV lower.
0.7 V SS. Crosses at about 0.37 V, but this plot has the widest temperature spread: the -40 C curves cross near 0.43 V. Slow devices at 0.7 V sit closest to threshold, so the temperature dependence of Vt dominates. Cold SS is the limiting case for this corner.
0.7 V FF. Crosses at about 0.34 V, and the temperature curves stay close together. This is the least sensitive corner, and its margin is about the same as TT.
0.7 V FNSP, the worst hold case of all your runs. Crosses at about 0.24 V, and about 0.21 V when hot. The ceiling is about 0.24 V (34 percent of VDD), and after the knee loss the real HSNM is likely under 0.2 V. A fast PD and a slow PU drag the trip point toward ground.
0.7 V SNFP. Crosses at about 0.46 V, now above VDD/2. The ceiling is VDD − Vm, about 0.24 V, so it is as bad as FNSP but from the opposite side. Here cold is the worst case, because it puts the crossing highest.
1.0 V TT, the reference case. Crosses at about 0.48 V, the lobes are close to square, and HSNM is about 0.38 V by eye. Compare every other plot against this one.
1.0 V SS. Crosses at about 0.50 V, centered, with sharp knees. Slowing both devices keeps them balanced, which gives the best hold margin at 1.0 V.
1.0 V FF. Crosses at about 0.46 V, and the knees are slightly softer, meaning lower inverter gain. Its margin is a little below TT.
1.0 V FNSP. Crosses at about 0.33 to 0.38 V across temperature, lowest when hot. The ceiling is about 0.36 V, so this is the worst corner at 1.0 V.
1.0 V SNFP. Crosses at about 0.60 to 0.63 V, highest when cold. The ceiling is about 0.39 V.
1.3 V TT. Crosses at about 0.58 V, below VDD/2 (0.65 V). The strong PD and weak PU from the beta sizing pull the trip point down, for a ceiling of about 0.58 V (45 percent). The transitions are steep, because the gain is high at this VDD.
1.3 V SS. Crosses at about 0.60 V, a little closer to center than TT.
1.3 V FF. Crosses at about 0.55 V. This is the most off-center of the symmetric corners at 1.3 V, at 42 percent.
1.3 V FNSP. Crosses at about 0.47 V, for a ceiling of 36 percent of VDD, so it is still the worst corner.
1.3 V SNFP. Crosses at about 0.70 V, close to VDD/2, for a ceiling of about 0.60 V. The stronger PMOS cancels the beta skew at this VDD, which is why SNFP is the best-centered corner here, even though it is a bad corner at 0.7 V.

Design guide

In practice nobody designs the bitcell from scratch: the foundry delivers it as a pushed-rule layout with its own models and sigma data. Your job as a circuit designer is the periphery and the assists that make that cell meet Vmin, speed and yield.

Cell sizing order (if you do size it)

  1. Pick L near minimum for density; PU and PG are usually minimum width.

  2. Set PD width for beta, check RSNM at mean-6sigma at the worst corner.

  3. Check WM at mean-6sigma with the strongest PU corner and lowest VDD; if it fails, do not shrink PD, add a write assist.

  4. Check hold SNM and DRV, then Iread low tail against the sense budget, then leakage at FF hot.

  5. Iterate with the assists in the loop; the assist strength is a knob just like a width.

Layout rules of thumb

  • Thin-cell layout with both PGs and PDs symmetric, so mismatch is random rather than systematic.

  • Mirror cells across the array so BL, VDD and VSS contacts are shared; mind edge and dummy cells at array borders.

  • Watch well proximity and stress effects; the corner cells of an array behave differently.

Read assists (improve RSNM, cost speed or power)

  • WL underdrive: lower V(WL) weakens PG, so the read bump shrinks. Costs Iread.

  • Negative VSS or raised cell VDD during read: strengthens the latch relative to PG.

  • BL precharge lowered (e.g. VDD - Vt): less pull-up from BL on the '0' node.

  • Short WL pulse (pulsed WL, self-timed via replica column) limits the time a disturb has to develop.

Write assists (improve WM)

  • Negative BL: drive the low BL below 0 V (e.g. -100 to -200 mV with a boost cap) so PG gets more Vgs. Most common today.

  • Cell VDD collapse: lower the column supply during write so PU is weaker. Watch half-selected cells on the same column.

  • WL overdrive: boost WL above VDD. Hurts half-selected read stability on the same row.

The write operation and the WL knob, simulated.

Left: writing Q from 1 to 0. BLB stays at VDD, so curve A (thick black) is the ordinary read curve. As BL is pulled down, PG1 drags Q lower and curve B moves down and left. That squeezes the lower-right (Q = 1) lobe. At BL = 0.40 V the lobe is still there, so the cell would not flip. Near 0.25 V it closes, which is this cell's write margin. At BL = 0 V only the Q = 0 state is left, and the write succeeds with about 250 mV to spare.

Right: one knob with opposite effects. Lowering WL from 1.0 to 0.9 V (read assist) raises RSNM from 287 to about 320 mV but drops WM from about 254 to 155 mV. Boosting WL does the opposite. The two curves cross just above VDD, so no single WL voltage is best for both operations. That is why real designs separate them: WL underdrive or a lower BL precharge for reads, and negative BL or VDD collapse for writes. A negative BL of -0.1 V adds that 100 mV straight onto the write margin without touching read stability, apart from half-selected cells.

Periphery that interacts with the cell

  • Sense amp: latch-type, offset sigma sets the required BL differential. Offset is analog mismatch, so this is where analog sizing matters.

  • Replica bitline / self-timing: a dummy column of cells tracks process so the SA fires at the right time across corners.

  • Precharge and equalize, column mux, write driver, WL driver sizing (RC of a long WL).

  • Redundancy (spare rows and columns) and ECC convert a per-cell failure rate into an acceptable array yield.

When 6T is not enough

  • 8T: separate read port (two NMOS stacked, read BL). Read no longer disturbs the latch, so RSNM equals HSNM and Vmin drops. Costs about 30 percent area.

  • 10T and Schmitt-trigger cells for near-threshold operation.

  • Register files and multiport cells use more ports for bandwidth, not stability.

Does gm/ID apply?

Mostly no for the bitcell itself, partly yes for the circuits around it. gm/ID is a small-signal, bias-point method: you choose an inversion level to trade gain, speed and efficiency around a fixed DC operating point. A bitcell has no bias point to choose. Its devices swing rail to rail as switches, and every spec above is a large-signal ratio of currents at specific terminal voltages.

Why it does not fit the cell:

  • Every gate is driven by VDD or 0 (WL, or the other node), so the inversion level is not a free variable. You pick W, not gm/ID.

  • Read stability is a current fight between PG (saturated, Vgs = VDD - V(Q)) and PD (linear, Vgs = VDD, small Vds). That is a ratio of large-signal currents, i.e. a ratioed-logic problem, like a pseudo-NMOS gate.

  • The metrics (SNM, WM, Iread, Ileak) are DC sweep or transient quantities, not gm, ro or fT.

  • At L near minimum in a scaled node, the variation and short-channel effects dominate any square-law or gm/ID intuition.

Where the gm/ID mindset still helps:

  • Near-threshold and DRV. At low VDD the cell runs in moderate or weak inversion. The latch gain that sets hold SNM is roughly gm x ro of each inverter at its trip point, and gm/ID tells you why: in weak inversion gm/ID approaches 1/(n x UT), about 25 to 30 per V, so a minimum-VDD latch still has gain. DRV analyses use exactly this subthreshold picture.

  • Mismatch. Vt mismatch maps into current mismatch as sigma(dI/I) = (gm/ID) x sigma(dVt). Devices at high gm/ID (weak inversion) are more sensitive to Vt mismatch in current terms, which is why low-VDD SRAM has worse Iread spread.

  • Sense amplifiers. The SA is a real analog circuit: its input pair offset, regeneration time constant C/gm, and kickback can be sized with gm/ID and the gm/ID LUTs from the characterization notes.

  • Leakage. Subthreshold leakage scales as exp(-Vt / (n x UT)); the same slope factor n that sets max gm/ID sets how fast leakage grows with Vt reduction and temperature.

Interview soundbite: the bitcell is a ratioed large-signal latch, so you size by current ratios and verify by DC sweeps and high-sigma Monte Carlo. gm/ID returns in the sense amp, in near-threshold retention, and in reasoning about how Vt mismatch becomes current mismatch.

Interview questions with short answers

  1. Why is PD bigger than PG? So the read bump on the '0' node stays below the other inverter's trip point. That is the cell ratio beta.

  2. Why is PU the weakest? So PG can pull the '1' node down during write. That is gamma.

  3. Which is harder at low VDD, read or write? Both degrade; read usually limits in older planar nodes, write increasingly limits in FinFET with 1:1:1 cells and strong PMOS. Say that Vmin is the max of the three.

  4. How do you get RSNM from a butterfly plot? Plot VTC of inverter 1 and the inverse of inverter 2 with PG on and BL at VDD; the side of the largest square inscribed in the smaller lobe. Or rotate 45 degrees and take the max diagonal distance divided by sqrt(2).

  5. Why is SNM not enough for sign-off? It is a DC voltage metric; it ignores current drive and dynamic effects. N-curves and dynamic (pulse-width-dependent) margins are better, and everything must be evaluated at 6 sigma.

  6. How do you simulate 6 sigma? Not brute Monte Carlo. Importance sampling, statistical blockade, or scaled-sigma sampling, often with a tool such as Solido or Spectre's high-sigma MC.

  7. What is a half-select failure? A cell on the active WL but in an unselected column sees a read-like disturb during a write. Column interleaving and WL boost write assists make it worse.

  8. Name two write assists and their side effects. Negative BL (charge-pump area and reliability of PG gate oxide); cell VDD collapse (retention of half-selected cells on that column).

  9. Why does 8T fix read stability? The read path is a separate stack whose gate is the storage node, so reading never injects current into Q.

  10. How does temperature affect the cell? Hot: leakage and BL leakage up, Iread may go down or up near the temperature inversion point. Cold: write often worst because PMOS and NMOS drive shift differently. Always sweep -40 to 125 C.

  11. Why does the sense amp need a replica column? To fire the SA just when the BL differential exceeds the SA offset, tracking process, voltage and temperature instead of a fixed delay.

  12. Where does analog design show up in SRAM? Sense amp offset and speed, replica timing, negative-BL charge pumps, WL drivers, and the statistics of mismatch.

Optional hands-on: butterfly curves in your PDK

A four-step lab, reusing the AFS run scripts from the gm/ID characterization, would turn every section above into plots you can talk through.

  1. Hold and read butterfly. Break the loop, DC-sweep each inverter's input, overlay the mirrored VTCs with WL=0 and WL=VDD. Extract HSNM and RSNM; sweep beta from 1 to 3.

  2. Write margin. WL=VDD, sweep BL from VDD to 0, find the flip point; sweep gamma from 0.5 to 2.

  3. Corners and temperature. TT, FS, SF at -40, 27, 125 C; plot RSNM and WM versus VDD to find Vmin_read and Vmin_write.

  4. Mismatch Monte Carlo. A few thousand samples, fit mean and sigma of RSNM and WM, and extrapolate to 6 sigma. Then add one assist (WL underdrive or negative BL) and show how Vmin moves.

Stretch goal: a latch sense amp sized with the gm/ID LUT, simulated against the BL swing the cell provides.
